newsitem.title: USA: Weather delays U.S. Mars launch until Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Weather delays U.S. Mars launch until Thursday.

text.p: Bad weather forced NASA on Wednesday to postpone at least until Thursday the launch of a mission to Mars, the first of three visits to the Red Planet by international spacecraft planned this year.

Cloudy skies and rain had threatened the liftoff but in the end high upper-level winds grounded the Delta 2 rocket, which was to send the Mars Global Surveyor on its 345-million mile (555-million km) voyage to the Red Planet.

"The launch has been postponed ... at about one minute, six seconds prior to launch due to upper level winds," NASA launch commentator Bruce Buckingham said. Launch from Cape Canaveral was rescheduled for about noon EST (1700 GMT) on Thursday.
The U.S. space agency had 20 days to get the probe off the launch pad or face a wait of 26 months for the planets to realign.

The spacecraft was designed and built in record time to replace NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which spun out of control just days before it was due to enter the planet's orbit in 1993. Surveyor carries copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on its ill-fated predecessor but at $215 million is much less expensive.

The probe is due to slip into an egg-shapped orbit around Mars in September 1997. It will then lower and circularize its orbit by dipping into the Red Planet's thin atmosphere and using its wing-like solar panels as brakes.

From an altitude of 230 miles (367 km) its telephoto camera will see objects on the surface as small as a compact car. By the end of one Martian year, 687 Earth days, 99 percent of the planet will have been mapped by Surveyor's electronic eye.
The probe does not carry any instruments that could directly detect evidence of life but it may scout out sites for a future mission to recover samples of rock.

Surveyor is the first of three spacecraft, two U.S. and one Russian, destined for the Red Planet this year. NASA plans to send pairs of spacecraft every 26 months through 2005 but has said it has no firm plans to send people to Mars.
Mars Global Surveyor was being launched amid revelations by scientists of possible ancient life on Mars and plans by two New York auction houses to sell fragments of meteorites from the Red Planet.

One of the auction houses, Guernsey's, estimated that three rocks that range from the size of a grapefruit to the size of a golf ball would sell for as much as $2 million when they go on sale on Nov. 20. Separately, Phillips auction house plans to sell three fragments of meteorites from Mars as part of a natural history auction on Dec. 14.
U.S. geologists announced in August they had found possibly life-related compounds in remains of a Martian meteorite that fell to Earth about 13,000 years ago.
